title: Understanding the UX Designer Salary in Australia: From Hourly Rates to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to calculate a UX designer salary from hourly rates, including award minimums, casual loading, tax, and super. Use our timesheet tool to estimate your take-home pay.
salarySummary: A UX designer on the Professional Employees Award 2020 earns at least the award rate, which from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour (National Minimum Wage) for a 38-hour week, or $1,004.90 per week, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: What is the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026?
faqs.a: From the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week, as set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Award minimum wages increased by 4.75% on the same date.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied to a UX designer salary?
faqs.a: Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 becomes $33.05 per hour for casuals. When using our timesheet, check the 'casual loading' box to add 25% to your base rate – do not enter a rate that already includes loading.

faqs.q: What tax and super are deducted from a UX designer salary?
faqs.a: For 2026–27, resident tax rates are: nil up to $18,200; 15% from $18,201 to $45,000; 30% to $135,000; 37% to $190,000; 45% above that. Medicare levy is generally 2%. Super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Use the ATO fortnightly tax table for withholding calculations.

bodyMarkdown:
## How to Calculate a UX Designer Salary from an Hourly Rate

When you're negotiating a **ux designer salary** or comparing job offers, the first step is converting an hourly rate to annual pay. The standard formula is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. In Australia, the typical full-time week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. So for a full-time employee, annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52.

For example, if a UX designer earns $40 per hour, the annual gross salary is $40 × 38 × 52 = $79,040. This assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, and no penalty rates or allowances. If you work part-time, adjust the hours accordingly. Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool does this calculation for you.

## The National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates for UX Designers

A **ux designer salary** must meet at least the National Minimum Wage, which from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. However, most UX designers are covered by an award – typically the Professional Employees Award 2020 or the Clerks Award, depending on the role. Award rates are higher than the minimum and vary by classification. From 1 July 2026, award minimum wages increased by 4.75%, so check the specific pay guide for your award.

If you're a casual UX designer, you're entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the base award rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that means $33.05 per hour. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how to apply this correctly. Use the [pay guides](/blog) to find the exact rate for your classification.

## From Hourly to Fortnightly and Annual Pay

Understanding your pay in different timeframes helps with budgeting. A fortnightly pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For a full-time employee on $26.44 per hour, weekly pay is $1,004.90, so fortnightly gross is $2,009.80. The Australian Taxation Office provides a fortnightly tax table to calculate withholding from this amount.

Annual gross is the figure you'll see in employment contracts. But remember, your take-home pay will be less after tax and Medicare. For the 2026–27 financial year, resident tax rates are: nil on the first $18,200, 15% on income up to $45,000, 30% up to $135,000, 37% up to $190,000, and 45% above that. Medicare levy adds 2% (unless you qualify for an exemption). Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator can help you see what you'll actually receive.

## Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Super guarantee contributions are not deducted from your salary – they are paid on top by your employer. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So if your annual gross salary is $80,000, your employer must contribute an additional $9,600 to your super fund. This is not included in the hourly-to-annual calculation but is a key part of your total remuneration package. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more details.

## Using the Timesheet to Estimate Your UX Designer Salary

Our [timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It then calculates your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross pay, estimates tax and Medicare, and shows your super contribution. Remember: the annual figure is an estimate based on a constant 38-hour week. It does not account for unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, salary sacrifice, or HELP repayments. Always refer to your award or enterprise agreement for your exact entitlements.

## Comparing Offers: Hourly vs Salary

When comparing a **ux designer salary** offer with an hourly contract, convert both to an annual figure using the same hours assumption. A $50 per hour contract for 38 hours a week gives $98,800 annually. But if the contract is casual, add 25% loading – that becomes $61.25 per hour, or $121,030 annualised. However, casual employees don't get paid leave, so factor that in. Our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page shows typical earnings for UX designers based on ABS data.

## Key Takeaways

- Use the formula: hourly rate × hours per week × 52 for annual gross.
- The National Minimum Wage is $26.44/hr from 1 July 2026; award rates are higher.
- Casual loading adds 25% on top of the base rate.
- Super is 12% paid on top, not deducted.
- Tax and Medicare reduce your take-home pay; use the ATO tax tables for accurate withholding.

Always check the Fair Work Ombudsman's [pay guides](/blog) for your specific award, and consult the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for the latest rates.
